D018-D005_h001.question:
It’s been going on a little over a year now, maybe closer to a year and a half. Since the accident, anything that reminds me of it—sirens, screeching brakes on the street outside the school, even a scene in a movie—hits me really hard. My chest tightens, my heart races, and it’s like I’m back in that moment, thinking, “If I’d just looked twice, maybe it wouldn’t have happened.” I keep replaying it and blaming myself.

But it’s more than that. I’ve become… flat. I used to love my kids at school, loved planning lessons and silly crafts. Now I feel nothing, even when they run up to hug me or my husband tries to cheer me up. I’m just numb and oddly irritable; there’s this low boil of anger inside me that comes out over tiny things.

My concentration is awful. I lose my place while reading to the class, forget instructions mid-sentence. Loud noises in the hallway make me jump out of my skin. And I hear voices sometimes—commentary, like people talking about me or arguing—completely out of nowhere, not about the accident or anything specific. They don’t match the memories; they feel like something separate and wrong.
D018-D005_h001.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h002.question:
It’s been a little over a year since everything started feeling…wrong. I used to really enjoy my job testing games, but now I can’t seem to feel much of anything—no excitement when a new build drops, no real fun even when I play for myself. It’s like the part of me that felt happy or close to people just shut off.

I do get really worked up when something reminds me of what happened with my ex and that night he grabbed me—if someone raises their voice, or if I see a scene in a game that looks like it, I get this intense, sick feeling and this rush of anger. I catch myself blaming him, my old friends, even myself, and I walk around simmering, snapping at coworkers over tiny bugs.

My memory’s been awful; I’ll forget what task I was doing mid-test or where I put my controller. Loud sounds in the office—like someone dropping a headset—make me jump out of my skin.

What really scares me, though, is the voices. I hear people commenting on me, laughing, or saying I’m useless when I’m alone, even in quiet, safe places. They’re not about that night, not flashbacks—just random, like a separate horror game running in my head.
D018-D005_h002.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h003.question:
I’ve been struggling for about a year now. It started after that car accident on the freeway—no one died, but a student of mine was badly injured and I still see it in my head. The scene just pops in, like a video on loop: the crunch of metal, his face, the smell of gasoline. I can be in the middle of lecturing on fluid mechanics and suddenly I’m back there. I keep telling myself I should’ve reacted faster, braked sooner, taken another route. I can’t shake this feeling that it was my fault, and I’m honestly ashamed even being around his classmates.

At the same time, it’s like all the color has drained out of my life. I go through the motions with my wife and kids, but I don’t really feel joy, even when objectively good things happen—like my promotion. My thinking feels foggy, like I’m wading through molasses, which is terrifying for someone who’s supposed to be sharp. When someone touches my shoulder unexpectedly, I jump out of my skin.

What really worries me, though, are the voices. They’re not about the accident—they just comment on what I’m doing, argue with each other about me, like a running commentary totally separate from those crash memories. Sometimes I’m convinced colleagues are planting devices in my office to record my thoughts, and I catch myself rearranging the ceiling tiles or checking the vents during office hours.
D018-D005_h003.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h004.question:
It’s been going on a few years now, getting steadily worse since the car crash on set. I still get these flashes of it in my head—the sound of the impact, the stuntman screaming—but they just pop in, like someone splicing jump cuts into my day. I can be watching dailies and suddenly I’m right back there.

Since then I’ve pulled away from a lot of things I used to love—going to festivals, even watching movies for pleasure. I go through the motions for work, but it feels flat. I keep circling around this idea that the producers, the studio, even the crew are to blame—that if they’d listened to me about safety, none of it would’ve happened. And the terror of that day just hangs around; it doesn’t fade. It’s like a permanent background hum.

On top of that, I’ve started hearing this man’s voice commenting on my choices, criticizing my shots, even when I’m alone at home—not related to the crash at all. Sometimes I see shadows moving in the corners that no one else notices. I get weirdly stuck on tiny decisions—what to wear to set, what to order—like I’m paralyzed. And if someone slams a door or drops something, my heart races and my hands shake for ages before I can pull myself together again.
D018-D005_h004.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h005.question:
It’s been getting worse over the past couple of years, but really noticeable this last year. Ever since my husband died, I keep having these awful dreams about the night he passed and the hospital. I wake up in a sweat, heart pounding. I keep thinking if I’d noticed something sooner, or pushed the doctors harder, he might still be here. I can’t shake this feeling that it’s my fault. I used to enjoy my garden, my knitting group, even visits from the grandkids. Now it all feels…flat. I go through the motions, but I don’t really feel joy or love the way I used to. Mostly I feel guilty and empty.

My memory isn’t what it was either. I’ll walk into the kitchen and forget why, or misplace my glasses three times a day. Sudden loud noises make me jump badly—if someone drops a pan, I flinch like I’m under attack.

What really scares me, though, are the voices. I hear people murmuring about me, sometimes laughing or saying I’m a burden, even when the house is quiet. They don’t seem connected to my husband or that night; they’re just there, commenting on me, and I know that isn’t normal.
D018-D005_h005.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h006.question:
It’s been about a year now since things really went off the rails. I was jumped outside a club one night and got pretty badly beaten. Since then, anytime something reminds me of it—like a similar alleyway or even just loud male voices—my heart starts pounding, I sweat, my whole body tenses up, like I’m right back there. I try hard not to think about it; if my mind even starts going in that direction, I shut it down, distract myself with training or scrolling my phone.

There are parts of that night I can’t piece together—certain moments are just blank—but I remember other bits way too clearly. Most of the time I feel kind of dead inside, like I’m going through the motions with clients, faking the enthusiasm. Things I used to enjoy don’t really register.

I’m on edge all the time—snapping at people at the gym over small stuff, and if someone walks up behind me fast or a weight drops unexpectedly, I jump like crazy.  

What really scares me, though, is I hear this male voice talking about me, criticizing me, even when nothing is happening and it has nothing to do with the attack. Sometimes I see quick shadows or figures in the corner of my eye, even in safe places like my apartment or the gym, and I can’t shake the feeling that something’s wrong with my mind.
D018-D005_h006.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h007.question:
I’ve been having a lot of trouble since that accident two years ago. Honestly, big chunks of that day are just… blank. My parents keep telling me details, but I can’t really picture most of it, like my brain refuses to pull it up. If something reminds me of it—like screeching tires in a movie—I’ll suddenly feel like I’m back there, not just remembering it but actually there, and I kind of lose track of where I am for a bit.

Because of that, I try hard not to think about it at all. If a conversation goes near that topic, I change it or leave. I avoid the route where it happened. But at the same time, it’s weird: I feel kind of numb toward my family. They say they love me and worry about me, and I know I should feel something stronger, but it’s like it’s behind glass.

I also get jumpy—when my boss walks up behind me in the studio, I flinch like I’m about to be hit. I snap easily over small things, yelling at coworkers or friends, then regret it.

Lately, I’ve been hearing a man’s voice commenting on my drawings, insulting me, even when everything is quiet. It doesn’t sound like anyone I know, and it doesn’t have anything to do with the accident. Sometimes I also catch glimpses of shadowy figures at the edge of my vision that disappear when I look directly.
D018-D005_h007.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h008.question:
It started after that car accident two years ago, but what’s bothering me now feels…different. I still get these awful dreams a few times a week where I’m back in the smashed car, or I just wake up with that same terror, even if I don’t remember the whole dream. Parts of that day are crystal clear—the sound of the metal, the smell of gasoline—but there are chunks I just can’t pull up, like they’ve been erased. I try not to think about it; if my husband brings it up or a coworker mentions car crashes, I shut down or change the subject.

What scares me more is that I hear a man’s voice commenting on what I’m doing—at school, at home—saying things like, “They’re judging you,” or “You’re useless.” He never talks about the accident; it’s like he’s just…there, running commentary. Sometimes I see shadows moving in the classroom corners that no one else notices. I’ve started snapping at my students and my husband over small things, yelling before I realize it. And if someone slams a door or a kid screams, my heart races and my hands shake for ages; I can’t settle back into teaching. I also feel oddly blank toward my husband—like I know I should feel close, but it’s as if something’s cut off inside.
D018-D005_h008.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h009.question:
I work grading diamonds, so I’m used to tiny details, but for the last year and a half my own mind feels like it’s slipping out of focus.

A few years ago something bad happened to me—I don’t like talking about it. When I even start to think about it, I shut down or change the subject. The strange thing is, I can’t really remember most of it clearly anyway; it’s like big chunks are just…missing. Sometimes, out of nowhere, I feel like I’m back there—my body reacts like it’s happening again, and I lose track of where I am for a bit.

Most of the time, though, I just feel empty, like all the good feelings are behind glass. I go to work, I look at stones, but it’s mechanical.

I’ve also been hearing a man’s voice commenting on what I’m doing—about the gems, about people on the train. It’s not about what happened to me; it’s more like a running critique that no one else hears. Sometimes I see quick shadows moving that vanish when I look.

I’m on edge, I jump if someone walks up behind me, and a few times I’ve snapped—shoved coworkers or slammed tools hard enough to break them when I get overwhelmed.
D018-D005_h009.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h010.question:
It started about two years ago, after that car crash on the highway. I remember parts of it really clearly—the sound of the metal crunching, seeing the airbag—but there are chunks that are just…blank. I’ll suddenly get yanked back into it, like I’m there again. I can smell the burnt rubber, feel the seatbelt digging into me. Sometimes it happens while I’m cutting a scene with traffic sounds, and I’ll actually duck or grab the chair like I’m bracing for impact.

I’ve been avoiding anything that reminds me of it—driving on freeways, action movies, even talking about road trips with friends. At work, even when I nail a really difficult sequence and the director’s happy, I feel nothing—no pride, just flat.

What scares me more is the other stuff. I hear a man’s voice commenting on what I’m doing—like, “You’re messing this up,” or “They’re watching you”—even when I’m at home alone, not thinking about the accident at all. Sometimes I’ll see a dark figure standing in the corner of the edit bay. If someone startles me, my heart races and my hands shake for ages; I’ve snapped and shoved coworkers or slammed equipment. It takes a long time to come down from that.
D018-D005_h010.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h011.question:
I’ve been struggling for about a year now. It started after that incident in the ER with the violent patient, but it’s gone beyond just that. I still get these episodes where I’m suddenly back there—like the room shifts and I feel like it’s happening again. Sometimes it’s so vivid I duck or try to get out of the way before I realize I’m actually in my office. Because of that, I avoid that wing, certain night shifts, even staff meetings where it might come up. I’ll walk the long way around the hospital just not to pass that area.

I’ve become convinced the world is basically unsafe, and honestly I keep thinking administration and security are the ones really at fault, like they set me up to get hurt and then just walked away.

What worries me most, though, are these voices I hear—like a running commentary about me, or saying my name when no one’s there. They’re not about the assault; they’re just… there, almost all day sometimes. I’ll snap at coworkers, yell or curse if I feel even slightly criticized. I know I’m more irritable and aggressive than I used to be, and it’s starting to cause problems at work.
D018-D005_h011.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h012.question:
I’ve worked in war zones and disaster areas for years, so bad images are kind of my job. But things changed about a year ago, after that car bombing in Syria. Since then I get these episodes where I’m suddenly back there—smell, sound, the whole thing—and I’ll duck down or start shouting before I realize I’m actually in my kitchen or the editing room. I’ve stopped going near newsrooms or talking to old crew; even certain streets in the city I avoid because they remind me of shooting locations.

I keep thinking the world is basically a rigged game—pointless, dangerous—and that if I hadn’t pushed so hard for that assignment, my sound guy would still be alive. That’s on me. When I lose it, I’ve thrown chairs, smashed equipment. My ex-wife left partly because of that.

What scares me most now is the… voices. I hear people commenting on what I’m doing, like a running critique of my life, even when I’m not thinking about the bombing at all. Sometimes I see shadows moving in the apartment, shapes that weren’t there. They don’t match any specific memory; they just feel like something’s wrong with my mind, beyond the trauma.
D018-D005_h012.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h013.question:
I’ve been on edge for a couple of years now, ever since the robbery at one of my restaurants. My heart still races and I start sweating if someone comes in late at night with a hoodie, or if I hear a loud bang in the kitchen. I try really hard not to think about that night—I’ll change the subject, keep myself overly busy with inventory, anything so I don’t have to replay it. When the memories creep in, I push them away because it feels like I failed my staff by not keeping them safe.

Since then I’ve started seeing and hearing things, but they don’t match what happened that night. I hear a man muttering my name in the walk‑in freezer when no one’s there, or see shadows moving along the ceiling at home. Sometimes I’m convinced cameras are hidden in my restaurants and that people are watching me, even my husband thinks that sounds paranoid.

I’ve become more convinced the world is just dangerous and pointless; it’s hard to see any good in people. I’ve snapped a few times—slammed plates against the wall in the kitchen and once shoved an employee when I thought he was “in on it.”
D018-D005_h013.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h014.question:
It started after my husband passed, about three years ago, but it’s gotten much worse in the last year. I still think a lot about the car accident where my sister died when we were young. When anything reminds me of it—sirens outside, a certain song on the radio—my heart races, my hands shake, and I feel like I can’t breathe. I try very hard not to think about it; if a memory starts to come up, I push it away, change the channel, get up and fuss in the kitchen.

I’ve come to feel like the world is just…bad. Dangerous. That there’s no real point to anything. I keep telling myself if I’d insisted we leave earlier that night, my sister might still be alive. I go over that again and again.

What worries my daughter is that I hear voices now. They’re strangers, men and women, commenting on what I’m doing, sometimes arguing with each other. They don’t talk about the accident at all. Sometimes I get so overwhelmed and irritable that I’ve thrown a mug against the wall or shoved my grandson when he startled me, which is completely out of character for me.
D018-D005_h014.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h015.question:
It started about a year ago, after that car accident. I still get these random, intense memories of it—like I’m back there hearing the crunch of metal—but I try really hard not to think about it. If anything reminds me of driving, I shut it down, change the subject, put on my headphones. I keep telling myself it was my fault, that if I’d been paying more attention nobody would’ve gotten hurt. Since then I’ve kind of decided the world’s just…broken. Like nothing really matters and bad stuff is just going to happen no matter what you do.

But what’s freaking me out more lately are these voices. They don’t talk about the accident; they just comment on what I’m doing, say my name, or tell me people at school are laughing at me. Sometimes I see shadows moving that no one else sees. I’ll suddenly snap and start yelling at my parents or friends over small things, swearing and blaming them, and then feel stupid afterward. It’s making it hard to focus on classes and finishing senior year.
D018-D005_h015.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h016.question:
It started after that thing that happened a couple of years ago. I still get these images popping into my head out of nowhere—like I’m right back there. I’ll be in the middle of editing a campaign or writing copy and suddenly I’m replaying it in my mind, and my body reacts like it’s actually happening. I try really hard not to think about it—if something on social media even vaguely reminds me of it, I scroll past fast or shut my laptop. I avoid certain places and conversations because I’m scared it’ll trigger those memories again.  

I keep thinking a lot of this is really my ex’s fault, or even my old boss’s, like if they’d acted differently none of it would’ve happened. I catch myself going over and over how they ruined things.  

I’m constantly on edge—when I’m out, I’m scanning people, exits, noises, like I’m waiting for something bad to happen.  

But there’s also… other stuff that doesn’t fit with that memory. I hear a man’s voice commenting on what I’m doing, saying I’m worthless or that people are watching me, even when I’m home alone and nothing around me is triggering thoughts about what happened. Sometimes I see quick shadows moving in the corner of my eye, or I get this strong feeling that the ads I’m scrolling past are sending hidden messages specifically to me.
D018-D005_h016.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)

D018-D005_h017.question:
I’ve been driving long haul for over 30 years, and about three years ago I had a bad wreck in a snowstorm. Ever since then, any time I see twisted metal on the road or even hear skidding tires, my chest tightens and I feel like I’m back there again. I go way out of my way to avoid that stretch of highway, and I’ll turn down loads if I know they take me near the spot. I steer clear of talking about accidents with other drivers too.

I keep thinking it was my fault, like if I’d braked sooner or taken a different route nobody would’ve been hurt. I replay that in my head a lot.

On top of that, for the past couple of years I’ve been hearing this male voice talking about me, commenting on what I’m doing, even when I’m just sitting in my cab. It doesn’t talk about the crash; it’s more like it criticizes me or laughs at me. Sometimes I think I see shadows or figures in my mirrors that aren’t there. I find myself constantly scanning truck stops, checking exits and watching people, just making sure everything’s safe.
D018-D005_h017.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizophrenia

D018-D005_h018.question:
It started after I retired, about three years ago. I keep thinking back to that robbery at the office in the 80s when the guy pulled a gun on us. Those scenes just pop into my head, like a reel I can’t switch off. I try not to think about it—if anything reminds me of that day, I push it away, change the channel, leave the room. I even avoid talking about my old job with my wife or the kids. 

I keep going over it in my head, though, deciding if it hadn’t been for that young supervisor insisting we stay late, none of this would’ve happened. I get stuck there, angry at him, even though it’s been decades. 

Lately I’m constantly on edge. When I’m out, I watch everyone—who’s behind me, who’s standing too close. At home I check the locks several times a night, pacing around like I’m on patrol. 

What worries me most is the voices. I hear men arguing about me in the next room, saying I’m “useless” and “finished,” but they’re not talking about the robbery or that day at all. Sometimes I also feel like the TV is sending me special messages, like the newsreader is talking directly to me, which I know sounds odd.
D018-D005_h018.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizophrenia

D018-D005_h019.question:
I’ve been driving city buses for over 25 years, and ever since that crash about a year ago, things have gone downhill—but not in the way I expected.

I do get memories of the accident popping into my head when I’m trying to relax at home—the screeching brakes, the thud—but what’s scaring me more are these voices I hear that don’t have anything to do with that day. It’s like a running commentary, usually two or three male voices arguing about me, saying I’m useless or that people on the bus are watching me. They’re not talking about the crash; they’re just… there, even when nothing reminds me of it.

I’ve started avoiding driving past the intersection where the accident happened, and I’ll switch routes with a coworker if I can. I also find myself constantly scanning the mirrors, checking who’s getting on, where the exits are—over and over, even on quiet routes.

Lately I’ve been convinced some of the passengers are plotting something, like they’re connected somehow, and I catch myself blaming my supervisor for forcing me back to work and “setting me up” for another disaster. My wife says I’m more suspicious and distant, but I can’t shake the feeling something’s off and that people are against me.
D018-D005_h019.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizophrenia

D018-D005_h020.question:
It started after that car accident about three years ago. I still get these sudden, graphic memories of the crash—out of nowhere I’m back in the driver’s seat, hearing the crunch of metal, smelling the airbag. Those voices and ideas don’t seem connected to the crash; they’re just… there, and they’re getting harder to ignore.
D018-D005_h020.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Schizophrenia

D018-D005_h021.question:
It started after my husband died three years ago. I still get this wave of panic and sick feeling when something reminds me of the night he passed—sirens, hospital smells, even certain TV shows. It’s like my whole body tightens and I just want to run or scream. I feel so ashamed that I couldn’t do more for him, like I failed as a wife. That shame just sits in me all the time.

Even when something good happens—my daughter had a baby last year—I can’t really feel happy. I know I should, I smile and say the right things, but inside it’s just…flat, numb. People at the houses I clean say I seem “quiet” now.

Lately, there’s more that scares me. I hear a man’s voice arguing with me, calling me useless, even when I’m alone in an empty room at work. It isn’t my husband’s voice, and it’s not about what happened to him—it’s just there, out of nowhere. Sometimes I see shadows or faces in the corner that vanish when I look straight at them. When I’m on edge like that, I snap at people, yell at my sister or my boss over small things, really let loose with my mouth, then feel awful after.
D018-D005_h021.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)

D018-D005_h022.question:
I’ve been having these nightmares pretty much every night for the past year. They’re about the car accident I had on a delivery route—same screeching brakes, same crash. I jolt awake sweating, heart racing, and then I can’t get back to sleep because I’m stuck in that fear feeling. Even during the day, I feel constantly on edge, like something bad is about to happen. I’m always tense, jumpy, scanning the road and people around me.

What’s weird is that I also hear a man’s voice commenting on what I’m doing, like, “You’re messing this up,” or “They’re watching you,” even when I’m just loading packages. It doesn’t sound like the crash, and it’s not about the accident—it’s just there, out of nowhere, even when I’m not thinking about what happened. Sometimes I see shadows moving in the corner of my eye that no one else sees.

D018-D005_h022.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)

D018-D005_h023.question:
I work as a writer for a morning news show, so my head’s always full of deadlines and scripts, but over the last year things have felt like they’re slipping out of my control.

I did go through a bad incident a few years back during a live remote—someone in the crowd got violent—and even now, if I’m in a packed studio or I hear that same kind of shouting, my chest tightens and I feel like I’m right back there. It’s this intense rush of fear and I can’t focus on anything else for a while.

D018-D005_h023.options:

Ever since the fire we had at the restaurant two years ago, certain things set me off. I’ve been having these awful dreams for a couple of years now. They’re always about that car crash we had on the highway ten years ago—the screeching tires, my wife screaming, glass everywhere. I wake up drenched in sweat, heart pounding, and it takes me a while to remember I’m in my own bed, that we survived.

Even during the day, I feel constantly on edge, like something terrible is about to happen. My shoulders are always tight, I’m jumpy at the slightest noise. I still write, but when I finish a chapter or get praise from my editor, there’s just nothing there—no sense of pleasure or pride, just a sort of dull emptiness.

What worries my wife most is how I’ve been lashing out. I’ve shoved her away when she tried to wake me, and once I slammed my laptop against the wall because the email notification startled me.
